name: UGC NET Paper 1
fullName: UGC National Eligibility Test – Paper 1 (General Paper on Teaching & Research Aptitude)
conductingBody: National Testing Agency (NTA) on behalf of the University Grants Commission
frequency: Twice a year (June and December cycles)
approxCandidates: ≈7–11 lakh registrations per cycle (2024–26). Paper 1 is common to all 80+ subjects.
eligibility: Master's degree (or final year) with 55% (50% for OBC-NCL/SC/ST/PwD/third gender), or a 4-year UG degree with 75%. JRF upper age limit is 30 years (with relaxations). No upper age limit for Assistant Professor or PhD admission.

notification.summary: NTA released the UGC-NET December 2026 information bulletin on 8 Oct 2026. Online applications are open until 28 Oct 2026, and the CBT is scheduled for 14–19 Dec 2026. In the previous June 2026 cycle, results for 84 subjects were declared by late August 2026, with more than 4,000 candidates qualifying for JRF. Fresh exams were held on 9–10 Sep 2026 for English, Commerce and Sociology after errors were found in those papers. Dates come from the bulletin and news reports via web search; the ugcnet.nta.nic.in portal itself could not be reached from the research sandbox.

pattern.notes: In the real exam, Paper 1 (50 Q, 100 marks) and Paper 2 (100 Q, 200 marks) are taken together in one 3-hour sitting with no break. Each question carries 2 marks and there is no negative marking. The 60 minutes shown here is a suggested allocation for Paper 1. Officially the 50 questions are spread over 10 units, typically about 5 each. Comprehension is usually one passage with 5 questions, and Data Interpretation is a table or chart with 5 questions. The question bank holds 60 original questions (6 per unit) for building mocks. Qualification falls into three categories: JRF + Assistant Professor + PhD, Assistant Professor + PhD, and PhD only.

trendAnalysis.summary: This analysis covers June 2024 (re-conducted as a CBT in Aug–Sep 2024), Dec 2024 (held Jan 2025), June 2025, Dec 2025 and June 2026. Paper 1 is consistently rated easy to moderate. Comprehension, DI, ICT and Higher Education are the most scoring units, while Logical Reasoning (Indian logic: pramanas and hetvabhasas, plus syllogisms) and Research Aptitude are the most time-consuming. Recent shifts include more NEP 2020, SWAYAM and Academic Bank of Credits questions in Higher Education, more matching and assertion–reason items, and chronology-based questions. Environment questions increasingly focus on SDGs, COP and India's net-zero commitments. The DI set is usually one table of 5–6 rows needing percentage or ratio calculations.

topics.topic: Methods of Teaching & Online Platforms (SWAYAM, MOOCs)

resources.notes: During each answer-key challenge window, NTA publishes the shift-wise question papers with provisional keys and candidates' recorded responses on the UGC NET portal (also reachable as ugcnet.nta.ac.in). Final answer keys are published with the result. Older papers (2012–2018, from the CBSE/NTA era) were archived on ugcnetonline.in. Coaching sites host compilations, which are not official.

questions.explanation: The levels of teaching are memory (Herbart), understanding (Morrison) and reflective (Bigge and Hunt). The reflective level is the highest and is problem-centred.

relevance.note: Reflective level-Hunt with Herbart/Morrison traps; NET levels-of-teaching item

questions.question: Which Government of India platform hosts MOOCs offered by Indian universities and national coordinators such as NPTEL, UGC and CEC?
questions.explanation: SWAYAM is India's national MOOC platform. Shodhganga is a thesis repository, and Vidwan and IRINS are databases of experts and research profiles.

relevance.note: SWAYAM vs IRINS/Vidwan/Shodhganga INFLIBNET traps; recent NET ICT-in-education style

questions.question: In the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson & Krathwohl, 2001), which is the highest level of the cognitive domain?
questions.explanation: The revised order is Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. 'Create' replaced 'Synthesis' and became the top level.

relevance.note: Revised Bloom highest level Creating vs Evaluating trap; NET favourite

questions.question: A researcher compares the Class V scores of children who did and did not attend pre-school. Pre-school attendance has already happened and is not manipulated. This design is:
questions.explanation: When the independent variable has already occurred and cannot be manipulated, the design is ex post facto (causal-comparative).

relevance.note: Non-manipulated past factor -> ex post facto; NET research-method item

questions.question: Rejecting a null hypothesis when it is actually true is known as:
questions.explanation: A Type I error (α) is a false rejection of a true null hypothesis. A Type II error (β) is failing to reject a false null hypothesis.

relevance.note: Type I error definition with Type II trap; NET hypothesis item

questions.question: Under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018, similarity up to what level is treated as 'Level 0' and attracts no penalty?
questions.explanation: The levels are: up to 10% = Level 0 (minor, no penalty), 10–40% = Level 1, 40–60% = Level 2, and above 60% = Level 3.

relevance.note: UGC 2018 plagiarism Level 0 up to 10%; asked in NET research ethics

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"For most of human history, knowledge travelled by word of mouth. Epics, genealogies and medicinal recipes were preserved not in libraries but in memory, recited by trained specialists who treated accuracy as a sacred duty. Scholars once dismissed such oral traditions as unreliable, assuming that every retelling must distort the original. Field studies in the twentieth century challenged this view. Researchers found that some communities transmitted long texts across centuries with remarkable fidelity, using rhythm, repetition and strict teacher–student lineages as safeguards. At the same time, oral cultures were never frozen: storytellers adapted episodes to their audiences, adding local heroes or contemporary jokes while keeping the core intact. Writing, when it arrived, did not simply replace memory; it changed what people thought worth remembering. Once a text could be consulted on a shelf, the effort of memorisation seemed wasteful, and the specialist reciter slowly lost his social standing. Today, as digital search makes even written reference instant, some educators worry that a similar shift is under way – not the loss of knowledge itself, but the loss of the habit of holding knowledge within oneself."

Earlier scholars dismissed oral traditions as unreliable because they assumed that:
options: Writing had existed before oral traditions
Oral texts were too short to be useful
Every retelling must distort the original
questions.explanation: The passage says scholars dismissed oral traditions 'assuming that every retelling must distort the original'.

relevance.note: Factual retrieval from passage; passage shorter than NET's ~400 words

questions.question: Find the next number in the series: 3, 7, 15, 31, 63, ?

questions.question: Find the next letter in the series: B, E, I, N, ?

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Cities have always been engines of opportunity, but they are also becoming the front line of climate risk. More than half of the world's people now live in urban areas, and the share is still rising. Dense concentrations of concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, producing what scientists call the urban heat island effect. On summer nights, the centre of a large city can remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. The consequences are not evenly shared. Wealthier neighbourhoods often enjoy tree-lined streets, parks and air-conditioned homes, while informal settlements are packed with tin-roofed houses that trap heat and offer little shade. For outdoor workers – street vendors, construction labourers, delivery riders – a heatwave is not an inconvenience but a threat to health and income. Planners have begun to respond. Some cities are painting roofs white to reflect sunlight, restoring lakes and wetlands, and protecting urban forests. Others are issuing heat action plans that shift working hours, open cooling shelters and send early warnings by text message. Such measures cost relatively little, yet they require coordination between departments that rarely work together, such as health, labour and urban development. questions.question:
Read the passage and answer.

"Cities have always been engines of opportunity, but they are also becoming the front line of climate risk. More than half of the world's people now live in urban areas, and the share is still rising. Dense concentrations of concrete and asphalt absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night, producing what scientists call the urban heat island effect. On summer nights, the centre of a large city can remain several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. The consequences are not evenly shared. Wealthier neighbourhoods often enjoy tree-lined streets, parks and air-conditioned homes, while informal settlements are packed with tin-roofed houses that trap heat and offer little shade. For outdoor workers – street vendors, construction labourers, delivery riders – a heatwave is not an inconvenience but a threat to health and income. Planners have begun to respond. Some cities are painting roofs white to reflect sunlight, restoring lakes and wetlands, and protecting urban forests. Others are issuing heat action plans that shift working hours, open cooling shelters and send early warnings by text message. Such measures cost relatively little, yet they require coordination between departments that rarely work together, such as health, labour and urban development. The deeper lesson is that adapting to a warmer world is as much a question of social justice as of engineering. A city that cools only its richest districts has not solved its heat problem; it has merely moved the burden onto those least able to bear it."

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from the NTA UGC-NET Paper 1 cycles of June 2024 (re-exam Aug–Sep 2024), December 2024 (held January 2025), June 2025, December 2025 and June 2026: NTA question papers with provisional keys where available, plus shift-wise memory-based analyses (PW, Careers360, Aspirant Mitraa) found by WebSearch. Official papers could not be fetched in full, so unit-level frequencies are estimates combined with the writer's own knowledge of recent NET papers.
